title: Functions with Ingredients (Parameters)
story: You wrote a `greet()` function, but it always says 'Hello, friend!' What if you want to greet different people by name — Alice, Bob, your cousin? You need to send information INTO your function.
why: Parameters let you customize what a function does each time you call it, making functions flexible instead of one-size-fits-all.
analogy: Parameters are like ingredients you give to a recipe — 'make me a cake WITH chocolate' vs 'make me a cake WITH vanilla'. Same recipe, different result!
try_it: Add an `age: Int` parameter to `greet` so it prints both the name AND age. Call it like `greet("Emma", 15)`.
tips: Parameters go inside the parentheses `( )` when defining the function — each needs a name and a type
Arguments are the actual values you pass when calling — `greet("Alice")` passes "Alice" as the argument
Parameter order matters — the first argument fills the first parameter, the second fills the second, and so on
common_mistakes: Forgetting the type annotation on parameters — `fn greet(name)` is missing `: Str`
Passing the wrong type — `greet(42)` fails because the parameter expects Str, not Int
